title: Critical role of cardiac magnetic resonance in the diagnosis of left-dominant arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy: A paradigmatic case in a recreational middle-aged athlete
case_prompt:
A 54-year-old recreational male trail runner (∼5 hours per week) presented with several months of palpitations at rest and during exercise. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, dizziness, syncope, stimulant use (including caffeine), illicit drugs, supplements, or recent infection. His medical history was unremarkable; he had no hypertension, diabetes, or smoking history. Family history included a mother who died suddenly at 72 (no autopsy) and a father who died at 60 of chronic illness. 

On examination, blood pressure was 124/81 mm Hg, heart rate 66 beats/min; cardiac and pulmonary exams were normal. Laboratory tests were within normal limits, with no elevation of creatine kinase or troponin. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm, normal atrioventricular and intraventricular conduction, and low QRS voltage (<0.5 mV in limb leads). 

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated nondilated ventricles and atria, preserved systolic and diastolic function, and no valvular disease. On exercise stress testing (Bruce protocol), he achieved 107% of maximum predicted heart rate, with isolated infrequent polymorphic PVCs suggesting both LV and RV origins, three ventricular couplets, and one monomorphic triplet; no PVCs occurred during recovery. 

A 24-hour Holter monitor recorded frequent PVCs (419 total, 0.5% of all beats), frequent couplets, and one 5-beat run of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia; the predominant PVC morphology was negative in both leads, with other morphologies also noted.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. A broad range of cardiac and systemic disorders was considered and tested for — “we performed tests to evaluate for hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart valve disease, hyperthyroidism, pericarditis, myocarditis, Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome, atrial fibrillation, mitral valve prolapse, sarcoidosis, dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Brugada syndrome, catecholaminergic ventricular tachycardia, ARVC, abnormal coronary arterial origin, or benign PVCs in response to stress and/or exercise.”  
2. Exogenous stimulant or supplement–induced arrhythmias were excluded because the patient denied their use — “He denied the use of doping and/or stimulants, including caffeine.”  
3. Myocardial inflammatory or necrotic processes such as myocarditis were considered but laboratory markers were normal — “blood test results were within normal ranges, with no elevation of creatine kinase or troponin.”  
4. Conduction system abnormalities including Wolff–Parkinson–White or Brugada syndrome were unlikely given intact conduction intervals on ECG — “The 12-lead electrocardiogram ... showed sinus rhythm, normal atrioventricular conduction, normal intraventricular conduction, and generalized low QRS voltage.”  
5. Common structural heart diseases were excluded by echocardiography demonstrating normal chamber size, preserved function, and no valvular pathology — “The 2D Doppler echocardiogram showed no significant abnormality, including nondilated ventricular cavities with preserved systolic and diastolic function, nondilated atria, and no associated valvular disease.”  
6. Arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy was strongly suggested by CMR findings of subepicardial fat infiltration — “marked irregularities were observed in the epicardial contour, mainly on the lateral and inferior LV surfaces, suggesting subepicardial fatty infiltration.”
